topic.subject: science
topic.title: Gravitation
topic.scope: universal law of gravitation, free fall, g, mass vs weight, thrust and pressure, buoyancy, Archimedes' principle

nodes.name: Mass, Weight and Variation of g
Force proportional to product of masses
Force inversely proportional to square of distance
g is independent of falling object's mass
Mass is constant across the universe
Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid

misconceptions.statement: Gravity only exists between planets or very large celestial bodies.
misconceptions.why: Students only hear about gravity in the context of Earth, the Moon, or the Sun in textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: Every object in the universe with mass attracts every other object with mass, no matter how small.

probe.question: Does a pen on your desk exert a gravitational force on you?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the pen is too small to have gravity.

misconceptions.root_belief: only large things have significant properties

misconceptions.statement: Earth's gravity ends as soon as you leave the atmosphere.
misconceptions.why: Students see videos of 'weightless' astronauts and assume gravity has vanished.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity extends infinitely into space, though it gets weaker with distance; astronauts are actually in free fall.

probe.question: If a satellite is orbiting just above the atmosphere, is Earth's gravity acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is in space where there is no gravity.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects in a vacuum.
misconceptions.why: Everyday experience with air resistance (feathers vs stones) creates a strong intuition.
misconceptions.fix: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration 'g' regardless of mass.

probe.question: If a 10kg iron ball and a 1kg iron ball are dropped together in a vacuum, which hits first?
probe.wrong_answer: The 10kg ball because it is heavier.

misconceptions.statement: Mass and weight are the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, people use 'weight' when they mean 'mass' (e.g., 'my weight is 60 kg').
misconceptions.fix: Mass is the quantity of matter and is scalar; weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass and is a vector.

probe.question: What is the SI unit of weight?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Your mass would change if you went to the Moon.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the feeling of being 'lighter' with having less 'stuff' in their body.
misconceptions.fix: Mass is a constant property of an object; only the gravitational pull (weight) changes on the Moon.

probe.question: If your mass is 50kg on Earth, what is your mass on the Moon?

misconceptions.root_belief: properties change when the environment changes

misconceptions.statement: A large flat board exerts more pressure on the ground than a small sharp nail if pushed with the same force.
misconceptions.why: Students associate 'larger size' with 'more pressure' because the object looks more imposing.
misconceptions.fix: Pressure is force divided by area; a smaller area results in much higher pressure for the same force.

probe.question: Why does a sharp needle pierce skin easily compared to a blunt rod?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the needle is smaller and has less resistance.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: The buoyant force on an object depends on the object's weight.
misconceptions.why: Students think heavy objects 'push back' harder against the water.
misconceptions.fix: Buoyant force depends only on the volume of the displaced fluid and the fluid's density, not the object's mass.

probe.question: Two balls of the same size, one lead and one plastic, are submerged. Which has more buoyant force?
probe.wrong_answer: The lead ball because it is heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: the object is the sole cause of the force

misconceptions.statement: Heavy objects always sink and light objects always float.
misconceptions.why: Observations of small stones sinking while large logs float are often misinterpreted by ignoring density.
misconceptions.fix: Sinking or floating depends on the density of the object relative to the fluid, not its total mass.

probe.question: Will a massive wooden log float or sink in a lake?
probe.wrong_answer: Sink, because it is very heavy.

misconceptions.statement: Objects lose mass when they are submerged in water.
misconceptions.why: Objects feel easier to lift in water, so students think the 'matter' has decreased.
misconceptions.fix: Objects only lose 'apparent weight' due to the upward buoyant force; their actual mass remains unchanged.

probe.question: If you weigh a stone in water, why does the scale show a lower reading?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the water dissolves some of its mass or makes it lighter.

misconceptions.root_belief: feelings represent physical changes in matter

misconceptions.statement: There is no gravity in a vacuum.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the absence of air with the absence of gravitational fields.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity is an interaction between masses and does not require a medium like air to act.

probe.question: If we pump all the air out of a room, will you float to the ceiling?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because there is no gravity in a vacuum.

misconceptions.root_belief: forces need a medium to travel

misconceptions.statement: The gravitational force between two objects doubles if the distance between them is halved.
misconceptions.why: Students assume a linear relationship rather than an inverse-square relationship.
misconceptions.fix: According to the inverse square law, if the distance is halved, the force becomes four times stronger.

probe.question: If the distance between two masses is reduced to half, what happens to the force?

misconceptions.statement: Fluids only exert pressure in the downward direction.
misconceptions.why: Students associate pressure with weight, which they know acts downwards.
misconceptions.fix: Fluid pressure acts in all directions at any given point within the fluid.

probe.question: Does water in a bucket push against the side walls?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only pushes on the bottom because of its weight.
